A content delivery network is a system of computers spread across many cities that store copies of websites and videos so people can load them faster. Normally, every request for a page travels all the way to one origin server, meaning the original computer where the website's files actually live. If that server is far away, loading takes longer. To fix this, copies of the content get placed on servers closer to people, called edge locations because they sit at the "edge" of the network, nearer to homes and offices rather than in one distant building. When someone requests a page and a nearby edge location already has a saved copy ready to serve, that's called a cache hit, and it means the answer arrives almost instantly, without a long trip back to the origin. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood bakeries that all sell bread baked at one central factory, so instead of ordering from the factory every time, most customers just walk to the closest shop and get a fresh loaf already sitting on the shelf. This setup reduces waiting time, spreads out heavy traffic so no single server gets overwhelmed, and keeps things running smoothly even during busy periods. It also adds protection, since attackers trying to overload a website must contend with many spread-out locations instead of one weak point.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Origin server | The original computer storing a website's real files | It's the ultimate source when no nearby copy exists |
| Edge location | A server placed close to everyday users | It shortens the distance content has to travel |
| Cache hit | A request answered by a saved copy | It makes loading much faster |
| Content delivery network | A network of edge locations working together | It keeps popular websites fast and reliable worldwide |
